subject: Plots of population-level predictions from a random coefficients GLMM

messages.author: 81fa0134ef9b66e4
messages.subject: Plots of population-level predictions from a random coefficients GLMM
parts:
I trying to fit a logistic regression model with random coefficients. I don't have any trouble fitting the model but I'm interested in producing plots that show, for example, predicted y over the range of precipitation in the data. I can produce prediction curves by incorporating extra rows in the data (where y=NA, as explained at r-inla.org), but as far as I can tell, that requires you to include values for the random effects, so essentially you produce a line for each level of the random effect. 

While that's useful, I'm also interested in plotting the population-level effect (from just the fixed effect with credible intervals). I'm not a trained statistician, so I apologize if I missed it, but I haven't been able to figure out how to do this. I'm ultimately hoping to have graphs that show both the variability in the random coefficients but also show the population-level effect. 

I included a dummy example below to show what I've done so far, including a data frame that can be used to generate predictions for one level of the random effect. You can potentially manually calculate the mean population-level effect (as shown below), but that of course does not include any measure of error. I would appreciate any suggestions for how to generate plots of the population-level predictions (not just plots of the fixed effect coefficients as seems the default in INLA). Thanks!

# generate data
n.groups <- 16
n.years <- 10
n <- n.groups * n.years
pop <- gl(n = n.groups, k = n.years)

prec <- runif(n, 0, 1)
N <- round(runif(n, 10, 50) )
Xmat <- model.matrix(~pop*prec-1-prec)

intercept.mean <- 1 # Select hyperparams
intercept.sd <- 1
slope.mean <- -2
slope.sd <- 1
intercept.effects <- rnorm(n=n.groups, mean=intercept.mean, sd=intercept.sd)
slope.effects <- rnorm(n=n.groups, mean=slope.mean, sd=slope.sd)
all.effects <- c(intercept.effects, slope.effects) # Put them all together

lin.pred <- Xmat %*% all.effects # Value of lin.predictor
exp.p <- exp(lin.pred) / (1 + exp(lin.pred)) # Expected proportion
C <- rbinom(n=n, size=N, prob=exp.p) # Add binomial variation

# compile data
occ.data <- data.frame(pop = rep(as.numeric(pop), C),
                       pop1 = rep(as.numeric(pop), C),
                       prec = rep(prec, C),
                       y = 1)
unocc.data <- data.frame(pop = rep(as.numeric(pop), N-C),
                       pop1 = rep(as.numeric(pop), N-C),
                       prec = rep(as.numeric(prec), N-C),
                       y = 0)
data <- rbind(occ.data, unocc.data)

# run model
form <- formula(y ~ prec + f(pop, model = "iid", hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1e-06), fixed = TRUE))) +
                  f(pop1, prec, values = 1:56, model = "iid", hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = F, prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.05)))))
mod <- inla(form, family ="binomial", data=data,
            control.fixed = list(
              mean = 0,
              prec = list(default = 1e-04)),
            control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, config=TRUE))
mod$summary.fixed

# data for predictions for one level of random effect
pred.df <- data.frame(pop=1,
                      pop1 = 1,
                      prec = seq(from=min(data$prec), to=max(data$prec), length=100),
                      y = NA)

# manual calculation for mean population-level effect
prec.vals <- seq(from=min(data$prec), to=max(data$prec), length=100)
output <- boot::inv.logit(mod$summary.fixed$mean[2] * prec.vals)
plot(output ~ prec.vals, type="l")
